facts.claim: Everest: highest point on Earth; summit rocks are uplifted ocean sediments full of marine fossils
Summit elevation: 8,849 m (29,032 ft), on the Nepal–China (Tibet) border
Summit conditions: winds over 160 km/h (100 mph), temperatures regularly below −30°C (−22°F), oxygen about one third of the sea-level amount
Still rising: about 2 mm (0.08 in) per year; fits evidence that the Indian plate is still subducting
Why Everest is the tallest and not a nearby peak: probably “just luck”
Himalayan-Tibetan Plateau: currently the world’s largest active continent-continent collision; formed when the Indian and Eurasian plates collided after the Neotethys Ocean closed by subduction
Indian plate: broke from Pangaea; moved north for about 80 million years before hitting southern Central Asia
Collision: began 50–60 million years ago
Convergence: 40–50 mm/year; about half absorbed across the Himalaya
Subduction: nonuniform; Indian crust underthrusts southern Tibet
Mantle flow: slow, driven by heat from Earth’s interior; this flow moves the plates
Interior heat: sustains plate tectonics, which shape Earth’s surface over billions of years
“Cold curtains”: cold sheets of downwelling material sink into the deep interior, imitating subducted slabs

Plate motion: can change abruptly; in a convection model, a reorganization took about 6–8 million years as heat built up around a mature downwelling until its buoyancy overcame the downward pull and pushed a plate off course

facts.section: Earth’s layers, structure, composition and minerals
facts.claim: Earth’s interior: crust, mantle, liquid outer core, solid inner core

facts.section: Earth’s layers, structure, composition and minerals
facts.claim: Crust: about 0–100 km deep

facts.section: Earth’s layers, structure, composition and minerals
facts.claim: Crust beneath the Tibetan Plateau: twice the global average thickness

facts.section: Earth’s layers, structure, composition and minerals
facts.claim: Base of the crust under the Himalayan collision zone: about 66–81 km deep, from seismic profiles

facts.section: Earth’s layers, structure, composition and minerals
facts.claim: Inside the Himalaya: faults slice through much of the crust, separating squished, buried rocks scraped off the Indian plate

facts.section: Earth’s layers, structure, composition and minerals
facts.claim: Crust under Everest: thickness needed to support its elevation is probably already somewhat at a maximum; any taller and it may move or change, causing the mountain to sink

facts.section: Earth’s layers, structure, composition and minerals
facts.claim: Mantle: extends to 2,900 km depth from the crust; seismic discontinuity at 410 km; top of the lower mantle at 670 km

facts.section: Earth’s layers, structure, composition and minerals
facts.claim: Minerals: 410 km boundary tied to the olivine-wadsleyite transition; a 420–440 km diamond inclusion holds garnet, 10-Å phase, ilmenite and liebermannite

facts.section: Earth’s layers, structure, composition and minerals
facts.claim: Outer core: liquid iron-nickel

facts.section: Earth’s layers, structure, composition and minerals
facts.claim: Inner core boundary: 5,100 km depth
Temperature: rises with depth
Earth’s heat: two sources, residual heat from Earth’s formation and the decay of radioactive isotopes such as potassium
Bottom of tectonic plates (up to 200 km deep): 1,300–1,500°C
410 km discontinuity: about 1,560°C
Top of the lower mantle (670 km): about 1,700°C
Base of the mantle (2,900 km): about 2,300°C; outer core: about 3,700°C
Inner core boundary (5,100 km): about 6,000°C, close to the temperature at the Sun’s surface
